--- title: Differential localisation analyses bibliography: ../course_refs.bib editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ::: {.callout-tip} #### Learning Objectives * Understand what is meant by **differential localisation** and why it is studied with dynamic (multi-condition) correlation profiling experiments * Know the difference between the **BANDLE** and **SANDLE** approaches to differential localisation, and when you might choose each * Separate the two questions of a dynamic experiment: **where** each protein is in each condition, and **whether** it moves * Use published localisations from the original study to describe where proteins are in each condition * Run the **marker-based** and **marker-free** SANDLE tests on a replicated two-condition LOPIT experiment, and combine and threshold the results to produce a ranked list of candidate differentially localised proteins * Combine the SANDLE results with the localisations to describe where candidates move, including to and from `"unknown"` * Visualise candidate movers using protein profiles, spatial maps and alluvial plots, and critically assess the evidence for movement ::: ## From static maps to dynamic experiments In the previous lessons we generated a **static** spatial map: for a single condition we used marker proteins and machine learning to predict where each protein resides in the cell. Whilst the steady-state localisation of proteins can provide vital information about function, these localisations are specific to the system of interest under the study conditions. Given the functional importance of protein localisation, the question naturally extends from profiling the spatial proteome of a single condition to **comparing the spatial proteome between conditions**. Correlation profiling methods have been widely applied to study protein dynamics in response to drugs, stress, signalling and differentiation [@Itzhak2016; @Orre2019; @Mulvey2021; @Christopher2025]. We say a protein is **differentially localised** (DL) if it is assigned to a different primary subcellular location (or *niche*) in one condition compared with another. Discovering these proteins is the main goal of a dynamic spatial proteomics experiment. :::{.callout-note} #### What does "differentially localised" mean in practice? A correlation profiling experiment measures the distribution of each protein across a set of biochemical fractions. If a protein relocates, its distribution across the fractions (its **profile**) changes shape so that it now looks like the profile of a different organelle. A change in the *amount* of a protein (expression) without a change in profile shape is not differential localisation. Such differences in abundance would not be discovered in a correlation profiling experiment since differences in abundance are removed during the row sum normalisation step. We use the term *differential localisation* instead of translocation since changes in the distribution of a protein can be due to changes in localised protein turnover (synthesis and degradation) as well as active movement of proteins. ::: ## The use-case data: insulin-stimulated adipocytes In this lesson we will use a dynamic LOPIT dataset of 3T3-L1 adipocytes [@Conway2026]. Cells were analysed under two conditions: 1. **basal** (unstimulated) 2. **insulin-stimulated** Each condition was profiled in **three biological replicates**, and each replicate was fractionated into **10 fractions** which were quantified with TMT 10-plex labelling. Replicate 1 of the basal condition was processed alongside replicate 1 of the insulin condition, and so on, which means the replicates are **paired**. Insulin signalling in adipocytes is a classic example of regulated protein trafficking. The best-known example is the glucose transporter GLUT4 (Slc2a4), which is held in intracellular storage vesicles under basal conditions and is rapidly delivered to the plasma membrane in response to insulin, allowing the cell to take up glucose. We should therefore expect to see some proteins moving in this dataset. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![LOPIT-DC maps the spatial proteome of 3T3-L1 adipocytes under basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. a) Schematic of the experimental workflow used. b) Venn diagrams of overlap in proteins identified across three replicates of LOPIT-DC in basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. Data for each condition was concatenated to give 4005 proteins in common across both conditions. c) Profile of organelle marker proteins across all 10 fractions (basal replicate 1 data shown, all replicates in Extended Data Fig. 1b). d) Principal component analysis (PCA) projection of concatenated basal data (n = 3 biological replicates) showing distinct clustering of organelle marker proteins. Each point represents an individual protein. e) PCA projection of proteins allocated to each organelle under basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. One point is one protein and points are coloured according to localisation.](figs/adipocyte_lopit.png){#fig-use-case2 fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## BANDLE and SANDLE In the workflow paper accompanying this course [@Hutchings2025] we used **BANDLE** (Bayesian ANalysis of Differential Localisation Experiments) [@Crook2022] to find differentially localised proteins. BANDLE is a fully Bayesian model, it uses Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior distribution of its parameters, and it outputs a differential localisation probability for each protein. It is powerful, but it requires the user to set priors, run several long MCMC chains (typically on a high-performance computing cluster), and check that the chains have converged before the results can be used. **SANDLE** (Statistical ANalysis of Differential Localisation Experiments) [@Crook2026] was designed to answer the same question quickly and robustly, and to handle more complex experimental designs. | | BANDLE | SANDLE | |---|---|---| | Model | Fully Bayesian (Gaussian processes + MCMC) | Robust mixture model + regression test | | Run time | Minutes to hours; HPC often needed | Seconds on a laptop | | Priors to set | Yes | No | | Convergence checks | Yes | No | | Needs markers | Yes | Marker-based test yes, marker-free test no | | Paired / multi-condition designs | Supported (two conditions) | Supported (two or more conditions) | | Output | DL probability + localisation predictions | DL probability + p-value / FDR (need to merge with localisation predictions from elsewhere)|
#### SANDLE combines two complementary tests: 1. **Marker-based test.** Using the markers, SANDLE models each subcellular niche in each replicate with a robust multivariate *t*-distribution. The centre and spread of each niche are estimated with the minimum covariance determinant (MCD), which is insensitive to outlying markers, and graphical lasso regularisation keeps the estimates stable when a niche has few markers. Every protein then gets a probability of belonging to each niche, in each condition. The **differential localisation (DL) probability** compares these probabilities between the conditions: it is the probability that the niche a protein belongs to in the basal condition differs from the niche it belongs to in the insulin condition. In other words, it reflects our confidence that a protein changes compartmental identity [@Crook2026]. The test is called marker-based because it uses the markers to build its model of the niches. 2. **Marker-free test.** This test ignores markers and organelles altogether. It asks whether the *shape* of a protein's profile changes between the conditions by more than we would expect from replicate-to-replicate noise. The result is a classical **p-value**, corrected for multiple testing to give a **false discovery rate (FDR)**. Whilst removing the requirement for marker proteins has benefits, a shift in correlation profile shape can only be interpreted as differential localisation when we don't expect major changes in cell morphology. For example, if a stimulation results in nuclear swelling, the entire nucleus (and all proteins within this organelle) could have a differential profile. The two tests capture different kinds of evidence: "is the protein assigned to a different organelle?" and "has its profile changed?". Together they give each protein a DL probability and an FDR, which you can use to rank and explore candidates. There is no single correct way to decide which proteins are differentially localised, you might threshold on the DL probability, on the FDR, on both, or on either, and the thresholds themselves are a choice. Requiring both tests to pass gives a short, conservative list with few false positives [@Crook2026], while thresholding on either test, or using looser thresholds, gives a longer list for exploration. The right choice depends on your biological question and on what you plan to do with the candidates next. ### Our approach: localisation and movement as two separate steps A dynamic experiment asks two different questions about each protein: 1. **Where is it?** In which compartment does the protein reside in each condition? 2. **Does it move?** Is there evidence that its localisation differs between the conditions? We answer these separately. For the first, we use the localisations published in the original study of this dataset [@Conway2026], which are provided with the data. For the second, we use the two SANDLE tests. We then combine the two: for each protein that SANDLE flags as a candidate mover, we look up where it is localised in each condition. You could equally produce the localisations yourself with a classifier, such as the SVM we used in Part 2, applied to each condition in turn. Using the published localisations lets us focus this lesson on differential localisation, and lets us compare our results with the original study. ## SANDLE setup SANDLE has not yet been released as an R package (but will shortly become part of the `bandle` package). For this course, all the functions you need are in one script, `sandle_functions.R`, which we load with `source()`. You will also need the `MSnbase` and `pRoloc` packages from Bioconductor, which we used in previous lessons. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("code/sandle_functions.R") ``` ::: The script provides the following functions: | Function | What it does | |---|---| | `split_by_replicate()` | Splits an `MSnSet` into a list of `MSnSet`s, one per replicate | | `sandle_markers()` | Marker-based test, returns a DL probability per protein | | `sandle_marker_free()` | Marker-free test, returns p-values and FDR per protein | | `combine_results()` | Joins the two result tables by protein | | `plot_marker_profiles()` | Quality control plot of the fitted organelle profiles | | `plot_dl_results()` | Plots DL probability against FDR | | `plot_protein_profiles()` | Plots the profiles of chosen proteins in both conditions | We will demonstrate the use of each of these functions in the rest of this lesson. ## Importing the data ### Why `readMSnSet2()`? In the previous lessons we started from precursor-level output, processed it in a `QFeatures` object, aggregated it to protein-level and then coerced the protein-level sets into `MSnSet`s with `as(..., "MSnSet")`, so that we could use `pRoloc`. In practice, you may have been given data that has *already* been processed to protein level: a table exported from Proteome Discoverer or MaxQuant, the output of a collaborator's pipeline, or a supplementary table from a paper. This data here was taken directly from supporting material of the @Conway2026 paper. We can read the table straight into an `MSnSet` with the `readMSnSet2()` function from `MSnbase`. The end result is the same kind of object (an `MSnSet`) that we created by coercion at the start of part II, and everything we learnt about `pRoloc` applies to it. :::{.callout-note} #### Reminder: the three parts of an `MSnSet` An `MSnSet` stores three linked tables: * `exprs()`: the quantitative data, with proteins in rows and samples (here, fractions) in columns * `fData()`: the **feature data**, with one row per protein and any information about it, such as marker annotation * `pData()`: the **sample data**, with one row per column of `exprs()`, such as the TMT tag, condition and replicate `readMSnSet2()` builds the first two from a single spreadsheet. We add the third ourselves. ::: ### Look at the file first Before importing, it is good practice to look at the column names of our data file so that we know which hold the quantitation and which hold the protein information. We read just the header row of the basal file using the `getEcols()` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getEcols(f = "data/adipocytes2025_basal.csv", split = ",") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Accession" "F1_Basal_rep1" [3] "F2_Basal_rep1" "F3_Basal_rep1" [5] "F4_Basal_rep1" "F5_Basal_rep1" [7] "F6_Basal_rep1" "F7_Basal_rep1" [9] "F8_Basal_rep1" "F9_Basal_rep1" [11] "F10_Basal_rep1" "F1_Basal_rep2" [13] "F2_Basal_rep2" "F3_Basal_rep2" [15] "F4_Basal_rep2" "F5_Basal_rep2" [17] "F6_Basal_rep2" "F7_Basal_rep2" [19] "F8_Basal_rep2" "F9_Basal_rep2" [21] "F10_Basal_rep2" "F1_Basal_rep3" [23] "F2_Basal_rep3" "F3_Basal_rep3" [25] "F4_Basal_rep3" "F5_Basal_rep3" [27] "F6_Basal_rep3" "F7_Basal_rep3" [29] "F8_Basal_rep3" "F9_Basal_rep3" [31] "F10_Basal_rep3" "Gene" [33] "Gene.description" "markers" [35] "Prethreshold.allocation.basal" "Allocation.probability.basal" [37] "Outlier.probability.basal" "final.localisation" ``` ::: ::: The first column, `Accession`, holds the UniProt accessions. Columns 2 to 31 hold the quantitation: 10 fractions for each of the three replicates, named by fraction, condition and replicate (for example `F1_Basal_rep1`). The remaining columns are information about each protein, including the gene name, the `markers` column and the localisation of each protein in the original study, which we will use later. ### Read the data into an `MSnSet` `readMSnSet2()` needs to be told two things: * `ecol`: which columns hold the quantitative data. Here this is columns `2:31`. These become the `exprs()` matrix. * `fnames`: which column holds the protein names. Here this is `"Accession"`. These become the row names (`featureNames()`) of the `MSnSet`. All other columns go into the feature data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} basal <- readMSnSet2("data/adipocytes2025_basal.csv", ecol = 2:31, fnames = "Accession") insulin <- readMSnSet2("data/adipocytes2025_insulin.csv", ecol = 2:31, fnames = "Accession") ``` ::: Let's check that everything went where we expected: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Check the data for successful import dim(basal) # Proteins x quantitative columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4005 30 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} basal[,1:5] |> # Check the quantitation (first 5 cols) exprs() |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` F1_Basal_rep1 F2_Basal_rep1 F3_Basal_rep1 F4_Basal_rep1 F5_Basal_rep1 A2A432 0.08745038 0.03030518 0.03174216 0.04225273 0.08121325 A2A5R2 0.05985686 0.02862720 0.03947083 0.05595315 0.12166558 A2A6A1 0.07206068 0.05689001 0.06826802 0.06321113 0.08343868 A2A6Q5 0.09399478 0.08964317 0.06309835 0.09530026 0.09878155 A2A8Z1 0.06351741 0.05962406 0.07480723 0.21082536 0.23186453 A2A9C3 0.03376313 0.09583943 0.15339625 0.28459391 0.11471487 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} basal |> # Check the feature data col names fvarLabels() |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Accession" "Gene" [3] "Gene.description" "markers" [5] "Prethreshold.allocation.basal" "Allocation.probability.basal" ``` ::: ::: The import seems to have worked. One thing that we notice from the `exprs` data is that the quantitation is already scaled between 0 and 1. This is because the file we have loaded contained normalised protein-level data, that is the correlation profiles. If you are using a protein-level data file output from a search engine then you will need to perform the row sum normalisation yourself, as we did in Part I. ### Add the sample data The `readMSnSet2()` function only reads the protein table, so the sample data is empty. We add it from a second, small file that describes each of the 30 quantitative columns: its TMT tag, condition (`Treatment`) and `Replicate`. The row names of this table must match the column names of `exprs()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Add sample metadata to the pData slots of our MSnSets pData(basal) <- read.csv("data/sampleInfo_basal.csv", row.names = 1) pData(insulin) <- read.csv("data/sampleInfo_insulin.csv", row.names = 1) pData(basal) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Tag Treatment Replicate F1_Basal_rep1 26 Basal 1 F2_Basal_rep1 27N Basal 1 F3_Basal_rep1 27C Basal 1 F4_Basal_rep1 28N Basal 1 F5_Basal_rep1 28C Basal 1 F6_Basal_rep1 29N Basal 1 F7_Basal_rep1 29C Basal 1 F8_Basal_rep1 30N Basal 1 F9_Basal_rep1 30C Basal 1 F10_Basal_rep1 31 Basal 1 F1_Basal_rep2 26 Basal 2 F2_Basal_rep2 27N Basal 2 F3_Basal_rep2 27C Basal 2 F4_Basal_rep2 28N Basal 2 F5_Basal_rep2 28C Basal 2 F6_Basal_rep2 29N Basal 2 F7_Basal_rep2 29C Basal 2 F8_Basal_rep2 30N Basal 2 F9_Basal_rep2 30C Basal 2 F10_Basal_rep2 31 Basal 2 F1_Basal_rep3 26 Basal 3 F2_Basal_rep3 27N Basal 3 F3_Basal_rep3 27C Basal 3 F4_Basal_rep3 28N Basal 3 F5_Basal_rep3 28C Basal 3 F6_Basal_rep3 29N Basal 3 F7_Basal_rep3 29C Basal 3 F8_Basal_rep3 30N Basal 3 F9_Basal_rep3 30C Basal 3 F10_Basal_rep3 31 Basal 3 ``` ::: ::: Our `MSnSet`s are now complete: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} basal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MSnSet (storageMode: lockedEnvironment) assayData: 4005 features, 30 samples element names: exprs protocolData: none phenoData sampleNames: F1_Basal_rep1 F2_Basal_rep1 ... F10_Basal_rep3 (30 total) varLabels: Tag Treatment Replicate varMetadata: labelDescription featureData featureNames: A2A432 A2A5R2 ... Q9Z329 (4005 total) fvarLabels: Accession Gene ... final.localisation (8 total) fvarMetadata: labelDescription experimentData: use 'experimentData(object)' Annotation: - - - Processing information - - - MSnbase version: 2.39.6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} insulin ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MSnSet (storageMode: lockedEnvironment) assayData: 4005 features, 30 samples element names: exprs protocolData: none phenoData sampleNames: F1_Insulin_rep1 F2_Insulin_rep1 ... F10_Insulin_rep3 (30 total) varLabels: Tag Treatment Replicate varMetadata: labelDescription featureData featureNames: A2A432 A2A5R2 ... Q9Z329 (4005 total) fvarLabels: Accession Gene ... Differential.localisation.result (10 total) fvarMetadata: labelDescription experimentData: use 'experimentData(object)' Annotation: - - - Processing information - - - MSnbase version: 2.39.6 ``` ::: ::: ### Splitting the data by replicate SANDLE needs one `MSnSet` per replicate per condition. The `split_by_replicate()` function splits our data using the `Replicate` column of the sample data (stored in the `pData`). Importantly, this function expects a column named exactly as `"Replicate"` in the `pData`. If it doesn't exist already, it is necessary to add one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Split each condition by replicate - generates a list of MSnSet objects control <- split_by_replicate(basal, rep_col = "Replicate") # basal treated <- split_by_replicate(insulin, rep_col = "Replicate") # insulin length(control) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(treated) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: We can use normal R `list` nomenclature to access the newly generated objects. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} control[[1]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MSnSet (storageMode: lockedEnvironment) assayData: 4005 features, 10 samples element names: exprs protocolData: none phenoData sampleNames: F1_Basal_rep1 F2_Basal_rep1 ... F10_Basal_rep1 (10 total) varLabels: Tag Treatment Replicate varMetadata: labelDescription featureData featureNames: A2A432 A2A5R2 ... Q9Z329 (4005 total) fvarLabels: Accession Gene ... final.localisation (8 total) fvarMetadata: labelDescription experimentData: use 'experimentData(object)' Annotation: - - - Processing information - - - Subset [4005,30][4005,10] Tue Nov 17 09:44:29 2026 MSnbase version: 2.39.6 ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} #### Replicate order matters for paired experimental design The replicates must be in the same order in both lists, so `control[[1]]` and `treated[[1]]` are the replicates that were processed together, and so on. The marker-free test compares each insulin replicate with its matching basal replicate, so it relies on this. If replicates were not processed in a paired manner, the order does not matter. ::: The marker proteins are stored in the `markers` column of the feature data. As in BANDLE, **the same marker list must be used for all replicates of all conditions**. As we discussed in Part II, if a protein does not behave as a marker across all replicates of all conditions, it cannot be used as a marker for any part of the experiment. The markers are assumed not to move between conditions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Check markers control[[1]] |> fData() |> as_tibble() |> pull(markers) |> table() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cytosol Endoplasmic reticulum Golgi apparatus 42 42 12 Lysosome Mitochondrion Nucleus 22 256 34 Peroxisome Plasma membrane Proteasome 14 31 19 Ribosome unknown 59 3474 ``` ::: ::: ## Exploring the data Differential localisation analysis relies on the same thing as static localisation: well-resolved subcellular niches. Before we run any test we should therefore look at each replicate. Here we use `plot2D()` to plot the first two principal components (the default) of each replicate, coloured by marker. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Set plot dimensions par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) ## Loop over reps 1-3 of basal for (i in 1:3) { plot2D(control[[i]], fcol = "markers", main = paste("Basal, rep", i)) } ## Loop over reps 1-3 of insulin stimulated for (i in 1:3) { plot2D(treated[[i]], fcol = "markers", main = paste("Insulin, rep", i)) } addLegend(control[[1]], fcol = "markers", where = "other", ncol = 2, cex = 1.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: We see clear, separated clusters for most organelles and a similar overall picture in every replicate of both conditions. Note that each PCA is computed separately, so the plots may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other. What matters is the relative position of the clusters. :::{.callout-exercise} #### Challenge 1: Assessing resolution {{< level 2 >}} In a previous lesson we used `QSep()` to quantify how well the subcellular niches were separated. Calculate the QSep scores for replicate 1 of the basal and insulin data and plot them. Are the compartments equally well resolved in both conditions? Which niches are least well separated? ::: {.callout-answer collapse=true} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Carry out QSep qs_basal <- QSep(control[[1]], fcol = "markers") qs_insulin <- QSep(treated[[1]], fcol = "markers") ## Plot QSep results par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(qs_basal, main = "Basal, rep 1") plot(qs_insulin, main = "Insulin, rep 1") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Overall resolution is similar in both conditions, which suggests that the data are of comparable quality i.e., resolution. This matters because if one condition were much less well resolved, we might see more apparent ‘movement’ simply because proteins are assigned less confidently. For example, if the ER and plasma membrane are well resolved from each other in one condition but not the other, there may be a large number of apparent movers between these compartments. However, resolution can also change for biological reasons. If treatment alters the size or density of an organelle, its sedimentation profile and separation from neighbouring compartments, will change. It is therefore worth comparing resolution per organelle as well as overall. If resolution for a specific organelle differs between conditions, this may reflect either technical variation (e.g. gradient quality) or a real change in that organelle. Comparing replicates within each condition and checking whether that organelle’s marker profiles shift between conditions can help distinguish these. Where resolution is reduced, protein assignments in that region are less certain, so apparent movements involving that organelle or its neighbours should be interpreted with caution. ::: ::: ## Step 1: Where are the proteins localised? The localisation of each protein in each condition, as published in the original study [@Conway2026], is already in the feature data of our `MSnSet`s, in a column called `final.localisation`. These localisations were predicted with BANDLE and then thresholded on the allocation and outlier probabilities so that only confident assignments were kept. All other proteins are labelled `"unknown"`, in the same way as after thresholding the SVM predictions in Part 2. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Check protein localisations per condition basal |> fData() |> as_tibble() |> pull(final.localisation) |> table() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cytosol Endoplasmic reticulum Golgi apparatus 331 408 138 Lysosome Mitochondrion Nucleus 80 600 129 Peroxisome Plasma membrane Proteasome 39 238 87 Ribosome unknown 236 1719 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} insulin |> fData() |> as_tibble() |> pull(final.localisation) |> table() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cytosol Endoplasmic reticulum Golgi apparatus 302 415 95 Lysosome Mitochondrion Nucleus 77 586 147 Peroxisome Plasma membrane Proteasome 37 205 79 Ribosome unknown 202 1860 ``` ::: ::: Let's look at the spatial maps of both conditions side by side. As in Part II of the subcellular mapping section, we use the combined data from all three replicates, so we plot the full `basal` and `insulin` objects rather than the per-replicate lists. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Define plot dimensions par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) ## Plot subcellular maps of combined data per condition plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal") plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin") addLegend(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", where = "bottomleft", cex = 0.6) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: A large proportion of proteins are `"unknown"`. This is expected: many proteins reside in more than one location, or in compartments not represented by the markers, as discussed earlier in the course. ::: {.callout-note} #### Why not take the localisations from SANDLE? The marker-based SANDLE test also calculates the probability that each protein belongs to each niche, and `sandle_markers()` reports the most probable niche in each condition. However, these probabilities are a step towards the DL probability, not a classification. There is no outlier or `"unknown"` class, so every protein is assigned to one of the marker niches however poorly it fits, and the model is not tuned or thresholded in the way a classifier is. We therefore take localisations from a dedicated classification, and use SANDLE for differential localisation. ::: ## Step 2: Which proteins move? We now run the two SANDLE tests on the per-replicate data. Neither test uses the final localisations: they give each protein a score for whether it moves, which we will combine with the predicted localisations in Step 3 below. ### Marker-based SANDLE The marker-based test is a single function call. `sandle_markers()` fits a robust *t*-distribution to every niche in every replicate, computes the niche probabilities for every protein, and combines them into a DL probability. We pass the two lists of replicates and the name of the marker column. The robust fitting step uses random subsampling, so we set a seed to make the result reproducible. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Run marker-based SANDLE set.seed(1) marker_res <- sandle_markers(control, treated, fcol = "markers") ## Check results head(marker_res) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` protein dl_prob is_marker niche_control niche_treated 1 A2A432 0.57586757 FALSE Proteasome Proteasome 2 A2A5R2 0.71444320 FALSE Cytosol Proteasome 3 A2A6A1 0.84145198 FALSE Ribosome Nucleus 4 A2A6Q5 0.90375951 FALSE Ribosome Nucleus 5 A2A8Z1 0.07412112 FALSE Endoplasmic reticulum Endoplasmic reticulum 6 A2A9C3 0.99182236 FALSE Lysosome Peroxisome prob_control prob_treated 1 0.5038873 0.5288237 2 0.5802071 0.5863211 3 0.3415311 0.4787456 4 0.6635241 0.3328648 5 0.9712861 0.9532214 6 0.5286807 0.3331390 ``` ::: ::: The output is a `data.frame` with one row per protein. The columns we use are: * `dl_prob`: the differential localisation probability * `is_marker`: whether the protein is a marker. Markers are given a DL probability of 0 because they are assumed not to move The remaining columns give the most probable niche in each condition and its probability. As explained above, we do not use these as localisations. Since the results of marker-based SANDLE are intrinsically related to the quality of the markers provided, it is good practice to visualise the markers that we used as input data. We look at the fitted profile (mean ± 1 standard deviation) of each niche in one replicate. Each organelle should have a distinct and reasonably tight profile. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## QC check - plot fitted profile of markers for each niche plot_marker_profiles(marker_res, replicate = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: These marker profiles look good. In practice, we would recommend doing this for each replicate of each condition. :::{.callout-note} #### How the DL probability is computed For each protein, SANDLE averages the niche probabilities over the replicates of each condition. The DL probability is then the probability that a niche drawn for the basal condition differs from a niche drawn for the insulin condition, $1 - \sum_k p_k^{\text{basal}}\, p_k^{\text{insulin}}$. A protein confidently assigned to the same niche in both conditions scores close to 0; a protein confidently assigned to different niches scores close to 1. Because the DL probability uses the full set of niche probabilities, and not just the single most probable niche, it responds to any change in how a protein's probability is spread across the niches. This includes a protein that leaves an organelle and ends up between several, or one that becomes partly associated with a second niche. What it does not see are changes in profile that leave the niche probabilities unchanged, for example a shift within a single niche. Note also that a protein that is uncertain in both conditions gets a non-zero DL probability even if it does not move, because two uncertain niche draws can differ by chance. ::: ### Marker-free SANDLE The marker-free test is also a single call. It needs no markers and no model fitting, so it takes well under a second. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Run marker-free SANDLE free_res <- sandle_marker_free(control, treated) ## Check results head(free_res) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` protein p_value fdr neg_log10_fdr F_stat RSS_diff 1 A2A432 0.5594732005 0.75571338 0.1216429 0.8882892 0.005704546 2 A2A5R2 0.0411199251 0.16354052 0.7863746 2.4662294 0.009056281 3 A2A6A1 0.1223651790 0.30139763 0.5208602 1.8186480 0.046431178 4 A2A6Q5 0.0480435196 0.17540045 0.7559693 2.3719371 0.037212747 5 A2A8Z1 0.0963270550 0.26333779 0.5794868 1.9586834 0.006347953 6 A2A9C3 0.0009028486 0.01708049 1.7674996 5.1593952 0.035569636 ``` ::: ::: For each protein we get: * `p_value` and `fdr`: the p-value from the F-test and the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted FDR * `neg_log10_fdr`: $-\log_{10}(\text{FDR})$, convenient for plotting * `F_stat`: the F statistic * `RSS_diff`: the difference in residual sum of squares between the two models, an **effect size** describing how much the profile changes ### Combining the two tests We now join the result tables output from each test by protein. We also add the localisation of each protein in each condition from Step 1. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Formulate final results results <- combine_results(marker_res, free_res) |> mutate(loc_basal = fData(basal)[protein, "final.localisation"], loc_insulin = fData(insulin)[protein, "final.localisation"]) ## Check results head(results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` protein p_value fdr neg_log10_fdr F_stat RSS_diff 1 A2A432 0.5594732005 0.75571338 0.1216429 0.8882892 0.005704546 2 A2A5R2 0.0411199251 0.16354052 0.7863746 2.4662294 0.009056281 3 A2A6A1 0.1223651790 0.30139763 0.5208602 1.8186480 0.046431178 4 A2A6Q5 0.0480435196 0.17540045 0.7559693 2.3719371 0.037212747 5 A2A8Z1 0.0963270550 0.26333779 0.5794868 1.9586834 0.006347953 6 A2A9C3 0.0009028486 0.01708049 1.7674996 5.1593952 0.035569636 dl_prob is_marker niche_control niche_treated prob_control 1 0.57586757 FALSE Proteasome Proteasome 0.5038873 2 0.71444320 FALSE Cytosol Proteasome 0.5802071 3 0.84145198 FALSE Ribosome Nucleus 0.3415311 4 0.90375951 FALSE Ribosome Nucleus 0.6635241 5 0.07412112 FALSE Endoplasmic reticulum Endoplasmic reticulum 0.9712861 6 0.99182236 FALSE Lysosome Peroxisome 0.5286807 prob_treated loc_basal loc_insulin 1 0.5288237 unknown unknown 2 0.5863211 unknown unknown 3 0.4787456 unknown unknown 4 0.3328648 unknown unknown 5 0.9532214 Endoplasmic reticulum Endoplasmic reticulum 6 0.3331390 unknown unknown ``` ::: ::: To see how the two tests relate, we plot the DL probability on the x-axis against $-\log_{10}(\text{FDR})$ on the y-axis. The dashed lines show the thresholds we will use: DL probability > 0.9 and FDR < 0.1. Proteins in the top-right corner are supported by **both** tests. Point size shows the effect size (`RSS_diff`). We also highlight in red some proteins that were reported as high-confidence movers after insulin stimulation in the original study [@Conway2026]. These include the glucose transporters GLUT1 (Slc2a1) and GLUT4 (Slc2a4), the insulin-responsive aminopeptidase IRAP (Lnpep), which travels with GLUT4, TXNIP, which regulates glucose transporter trafficking, the Akt substrate ZNRF2, and the uncharacterised protein C3orf18. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Store featureNames of POI known_movers <- c("P17809", # GLUT1 (Slc2a1) "P14142", # GLUT4 (Slc2a4) "Q8C129", # IRAP (Lnpep) "Q8BG60", # TXNIP "Q71FD5", # ZNRF2 "Q8BGK9", # C3orf18 "Q9WTP2", # SPRY4 "Q05512", # Mark2 "Q9JLN9", # Mtor "Q80TM9") # NISCH ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Plot tests against each other plot_dl_results(results, prob_cut = 0.9, fdr_cut = 0.1, highlight = known_movers) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} #### Recap: what each measure tells us | Measure | Column | Question it answers | Comes from | |---|---|---|---| | **DL probability** | `dl_prob` | How confident are we that the protein changes compartment? | Marker-based test | | **FDR** | `fdr` | Is the change in profile bigger than replicate-to-replicate noise? | Marker-free test | | **Effect size** | `RSS_diff` | How large is the change in profile? | Marker-free test | | **Localisation** | `loc_basal`, `loc_insulin` | Where is the protein in each condition? | Published classification (Step 1) | * A high **DL probability** means the protein's niche probabilities differ between conditions, so it has probably changed compartment. It says nothing about how large the change in profile is. * A low **FDR** means the profile change is consistent across replicates and unlikely to be noise. A very small but reproducible change can still have a low FDR. * A large **effect size** means a large share of the protein has shifted to different fractions. On its own it says nothing about noise, so a large but inconsistent change can have a large effect size and a high FDR. We use it to rank candidates and to prioritise them for follow-up. * The **localisations** tell us where a protein moves from and to. They do not tell us whether it moves: that is what the DL probability and FDR are for. A convincing mover typically has a high DL probability, a low FDR and a reasonably large effect size. In a differential expression analysis, the FDR and effect size play the same roles as the adjusted p-value and fold change. ::: How many candidates do we get with each criterion? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Count number of differentially localised proteins per approach c(marker_based = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9), marker_free = sum(results$fdr < 0.1), both = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9 & results$fdr < 0.1), either = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9 | results$fdr < 0.1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` marker_based marker_free both either 322 718 77 963 ``` ::: ::: The marker-free test flags many more proteins than the marker-based test. This is expected, because the two tests ask different questions. The marker-free test detects *any* consistent change in profile shape, including small shifts within the same organelle. The marker-based test asks whether the protein's membership of the niches defined by the markers has changed, so a change in profile only counts if it changes which niches the protein is likely to belong to. How you combine them is up to you. Here we take the conservative option and require both, which gives a short list to start exploring. For comparison, @Crook2026 required a DL probability of at least 0.8 and an FDR below 0.05 for this dataset. Challenge 2 looks at what happens with other choices. Our candidate list, ordered by effect size: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Filter candidates and then order by effect size (largest first) hits <- results |> filter(dl_prob > 0.9, fdr < 0.1) |> arrange(desc(RSS_diff)) |> dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, loc_basal, loc_insulin) ## Look at the top 10 hits head(hits, 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` protein dl_prob fdr loc_basal loc_insulin 1 Q9QXM1 0.9638762 3.059785e-02 unknown unknown 2 P17809 0.9379280 3.427718e-04 unknown Plasma membrane 3 Q9WTP2 0.9245449 9.242064e-05 unknown unknown 4 Q9WU40 0.9926458 9.327580e-03 unknown unknown 5 Q8BG60 0.9721408 2.759772e-05 unknown unknown 6 P63073 0.9453802 1.153048e-05 unknown Ribosome 7 Q64430 0.9989656 9.157403e-04 unknown unknown 8 P08122 0.9293315 7.006848e-02 unknown unknown 9 Q9EQH3 0.9055122 2.950607e-03 unknown unknown 10 Q8BJF9 0.9691362 6.864604e-02 unknown unknown ``` ::: ::: And how do the previously reported movers score? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} results |> filter(protein %in% known_movers) |> dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, loc_basal, loc_insulin) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` protein dl_prob fdr loc_basal loc_insulin 1 P14142 0.6897125 1.526390e-03 unknown unknown 2 P17809 0.9379280 3.427718e-04 unknown Plasma membrane 3 Q05512 0.5885429 9.056267e-01 unknown unknown 4 Q71FD5 0.9939860 1.856309e-03 Plasma membrane unknown 5 Q80TM9 0.5473357 1.010438e-02 unknown unknown 6 Q8BG60 0.9721408 2.759772e-05 unknown unknown 7 Q8BGK9 0.8914838 2.229997e-04 unknown unknown 8 Q8C129 0.6619904 1.194070e-05 unknown unknown 9 Q9JLN9 0.3728184 3.779413e-01 unknown unknown 10 Q9WTP2 0.9245449 9.242064e-05 unknown unknown ``` ::: ::: Most of these proteins are supported by both SANDLE tests, so SANDLE and BANDLE agree on them. All of them have a low FDR, but GLUT4 and IRAP have a lower DL probability. We look at why in the profile plots below. :::{.callout-exercise} #### Challenge 2: Choosing thresholds {{< level 1 >}} Thresholds are a choice, not a law of nature. Find how many candidates you get if you use a more stringent threshold (DL probability > 0.95 and FDR < 0.01) and a more exploratory one (DL probability > 0.8 and FDR < 0.2). How many of the `known_movers` pass in each case? ::: {.callout-answer collapse=true} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Apply filters / thresholds stringent <- results |> filter(dl_prob > 0.95, fdr < 0.01) explore <- results |> filter(dl_prob > 0.8, fdr < 0.2) ## Number of DL proteins using these thresholds nrow(stringent) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(explore) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 183 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Check how many of the previously reported DL proteins meet each threshold sum(known_movers %in% stringent$protein) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(known_movers %in% explore$protein) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: Loosening the thresholds recovers more of the known movers, at the cost of a longer list that will contain more false positives. Which you choose depends on what you will do next: a short list for expensive validation, or a longer list for exploration and enrichment analysis. ::: ::: ## Step 3: Where do the movers go? We now bring the two steps together. For each candidate mover we look up its localisation in each condition, and summarise the movements as a table of *from* and *to* compartments, similar to the `plotTable()` output of BANDLE. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hits |> dplyr::count(loc_basal, loc_insulin, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` loc_basal loc_insulin n 1 unknown unknown 53 2 Plasma membrane Plasma membrane 6 3 Plasma membrane unknown 4 4 Nucleus Nucleus 3 5 Nucleus unknown 2 6 Endoplasmic reticulum Plasma membrane 1 7 Endoplasmic reticulum unknown 1 8 Golgi apparatus Golgi apparatus 1 9 Golgi apparatus unknown 1 10 Mitochondrion unknown 1 11 unknown Golgi apparatus 1 12 unknown Nucleus 1 13 unknown Plasma membrane 1 14 unknown Ribosome 1 ``` ::: ::: You will probably find that many candidates are `"unknown"` in one or both conditions. This is not a problem with the analysis. A protein that moves is, almost by definition, often a protein that does not sit neatly within one compartment: it may be distributed between several, be in transit, or be in a compartment that is not represented by the markers. @Conway2026 found the same in this dataset, where most high-confidence movers were "undefined" in at least one condition. ### Types of movement To see this more clearly, we take all proteins that pass *either* test and classify each by what happens to its localisation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candidates <- results |> filter(dl_prob > 0.9 | fdr < 0.1) |> mutate( test = case_when(dl_prob > 0.9 & fdr < 0.1 ~ "both", dl_prob > 0.9 ~ "marker-based only", TRUE ~ "marker-free only"), move = case_when( loc_basal == "unknown" & loc_insulin == "unknown" ~ "unknown -> unknown", loc_basal == "unknown" ~ "unknown -> compartment", loc_insulin == "unknown" ~ "compartment -> unknown", loc_basal == loc_insulin ~ "same compartment", TRUE ~ "compartment -> compartment")) table(candidates$move, candidates$test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` both marker-based only marker-free only compartment -> compartment 1 0 7 compartment -> unknown 9 25 65 same compartment 10 11 381 unknown -> compartment 4 6 31 unknown -> unknown 53 203 157 ``` ::: ::: Each type of movement tells us something different: * **compartment → compartment**: the protein is confidently classified to one compartment in each condition, and they differ. These are the clearest candidates. * **compartment → unknown** and **unknown → compartment**: the protein leaves, or arrives at, a confidently classified compartment, but its other location is uncertain. It may move to a compartment that is not represented in the markers, become distributed across several compartments, or sit between clusters. * **unknown → unknown**: the profile changes, but the protein cannot be confidently classified in either condition. These are often proteins that sit between compartments or are in more than one location (i.e., multi-localised). * **same compartment**: the profile changes, but the protein is classified to the same compartment in both conditions. These may reflect partial relocation, where only a fraction of the protein moves, a shift within a compartment, or a change that the markers cannot resolve. @Crook2026 interpret proteins with strong marker-free support but a low DL probability in the same way, as "more complex or heterogeneous spatial reorganisation rather than simple compartmental shifts". We can now make the *from*/*to* table for all candidates. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candidates |> dplyr::count(loc_basal, loc_insulin, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` loc_basal loc_insulin n 1 unknown unknown 413 2 Mitochondrion Mitochondrion 135 3 Endoplasmic reticulum Endoplasmic reticulum 59 4 Nucleus Nucleus 59 5 Cytosol Cytosol 49 6 Plasma membrane Plasma membrane 38 7 Plasma membrane unknown 28 8 Cytosol unknown 22 9 Lysosome Lysosome 16 10 Golgi apparatus Golgi apparatus 15 11 Peroxisome Peroxisome 15 12 Ribosome unknown 13 13 Ribosome Ribosome 12 14 Golgi apparatus unknown 11 15 Mitochondrion unknown 10 16 Endoplasmic reticulum unknown 9 17 unknown Nucleus 8 18 unknown Plasma membrane 8 19 unknown Endoplasmic reticulum 5 20 unknown Ribosome 5 21 Plasma membrane Endoplasmic reticulum 4 22 Proteasome Proteasome 4 23 unknown Cytosol 4 24 unknown Mitochondrion 4 25 Nucleus unknown 3 26 unknown Golgi apparatus 3 27 Lysosome unknown 2 28 Plasma membrane Golgi apparatus 2 29 unknown Lysosome 2 30 Endoplasmic reticulum Plasma membrane 1 31 Golgi apparatus Plasma membrane 1 32 Peroxisome unknown 1 33 unknown Peroxisome 1 34 unknown Proteasome 1 ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-exercise} #### Challenge 3: Proteins leaving the plasma membrane {{< level 2 >}} Using `candidates`, find all proteins that are classified to the plasma membrane in the basal condition. Where are they classified after insulin stimulation? Which of the two SANDLE tests supports each of them? ::: {.callout-answer collapse=true} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Subset proteins that move from the PM to somewhere else candidates |> filter(loc_basal == "Plasma membrane") |> pull(loc_insulin) |> table() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Endoplasmic reticulum Golgi apparatus Plasma membrane 4 2 38 unknown 28 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Check which test supports these candidates |> filter(loc_basal == "Plasma membrane") |> dplyr::count(loc_insulin, test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` loc_insulin test n 1 Endoplasmic reticulum marker-free only 4 2 Golgi apparatus marker-free only 2 3 Plasma membrane both 6 4 Plasma membrane marker-based only 5 5 Plasma membrane marker-free only 27 6 unknown both 4 7 unknown marker-based only 16 8 unknown marker-free only 8 ``` ::: ::: Proteins classified to the plasma membrane in both conditions are not necessarily false positives. Their profile has changed, but not by enough to move them out of the plasma membrane cluster, which could reflect a partial change, for example a fraction of the protein being internalised. Proteins that become `"unknown"` after insulin have moved away from the plasma membrane cluster without being confidently classified elsewhere. Look at their profiles with `plot_protein_profiles()` (below) before drawing conclusions. ::: ::: ## Visualising the candidates ### Protein profiles Always look at the data. `plot_protein_profiles()` plots the profiles of chosen proteins in both conditions: thin lines are individual replicates, thick lines the mean, and the shaded band ± 1 standard deviation. We pass our two lists containing `MSnSet`s for each replicate. We then pass a vector containing the names of our proteins of interest (which must match the `featureNames` of our `MSnSet`s). Finally, we give labels for our two conditions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = hits$protein[1:12], labels = c("basal", "insulin")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: A convincing mover shows a consistent change in profile shape across all three replicates, with little overlap between the two conditions. Now let's look at two of the known movers. GLUT4 (P14142) is the classic insulin-responsive protein, and IRAP (Q8C129) travels with GLUT4 in the same storage vesicles. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = c("P14142", "Q8C129"), labels = c("basal", "insulin")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: Both profiles change clearly and consistently, which is why both proteins have a very low FDR. Their DL probabilities are lower because GLUT4 and IRAP are stored in specialised vesicles that are not represented by any of the marker niches, and both are `"unknown"` in both conditions. Their profiles change, but not in a way that clearly moves them from one marker niche to another. This is a good example of a protein giving a clear signal in one test and a weaker one in the other, and of why it helps to look at both. We can also look at the strongest candidates, by effect size, from each type of movement. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Select the top 2 candidates from each movement type top_by_type <- candidates |> group_by(move) |> slice_max(RSS_diff, n = 2) |> ungroup() ## Check the data top_by_type |> dplyr::select(protein, move, loc_basal, loc_insulin, dl_prob, fdr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 6 protein move loc_basal loc_insulin dl_prob fdr 1 Q9CQE7 compartment -> compartment Endoplasmic r… Plasma mem… 0.915 5.70e-4 2 Q9CRA5 compartment -> compartment Plasma membra… Golgi appa… 0.709 6.01e-2 3 Q99M28 compartment -> unknown Nucleus unknown 0.346 5.44e-2 4 Q62422 compartment -> unknown Cytosol unknown 0.00421 1.70e-2 5 P27661 same compartment Nucleus Nucleus 0 1.29e-7 6 Q9JIX8 same compartment Nucleus Nucleus 0 1.15e-5 7 P17809 unknown -> compartment unknown Plasma mem… 0.938 3.43e-4 8 P48428 unknown -> compartment unknown Cytosol 0.00277 3.77e-6 9 Q9WV86 unknown -> unknown unknown unknown 0.751 8.86e-2 10 Q9QXM1 unknown -> unknown unknown unknown 0.964 3.06e-2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Plot these proteins plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = top_by_type$protein, labels = c("basal", "insulin")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ### Movers on the spatial map Next, let's put a few movers back onto the spatial maps. We plot the PCA of the combined data for each condition, coloured by localisation, and add the movers on top using `highlightOnPlot`. We use the top four candidates from both methods, plus GLUT4 and Q8C129. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Save featureNames of protein of interest to annotate movers <- c(hits$protein[1:4], "P14142", "Q8C129") ## Define plotting dimensions #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 6 par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal") highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = "yellow", pch = 21, cex = 1.5) highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, labels = TRUE, col = "black", cex = 0.5, pos = 3) plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin") highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = "yellow", pch = 21, cex = 1.5) highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, labels = TRUE, col = "black", cex = 0.5, pos = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Here we see all movers in yellow, labelled with their accession number since the default for `labels = TRUE` is to use the `featureNames`. In some cases, it might be easier to compare the movers if each individual protein has its own colour and symbol.The `bg` and `pch` arguments of `highlightOnPlot` can be a single value (all movers look the same) or one value per feature of interest provided in a vector. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mover_col <- c("black", "red", "blue", "darkorange", "green3", "magenta") mover_pch <- c(21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 21) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal") highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = mover_col, pch = mover_pch, cex = 1.5) plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin") highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = mover_col, pch = mover_pch, cex = 1.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: We can also plot a legend rather than cluttering our plot with labels. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)) plot.new() legend("center", legend = movers, pch = mover_pch, pt.bg = mover_col, col = "black", pt.cex = 1.6, ncol = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: The PCA of each condition is computed separately, so the two maps may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other. A mover should sit in, or closer to, a different cluster after insulin stimulation. A protein that moves to `"unknown"` will often move into the space between clusters. :::{.callout-exercise} #### Challenge 5: Follow your own proteins {{< level 2 >}} Choose three proteins from Challenge 3, or from the different types of movement above. Plot their profiles with `plot_protein_profiles()` and show them on the spatial maps using `highlightOnPlot`. ::: {.callout-answer collapse=true} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Here we take the top protein of three movement types movers <- top_by_type |> group_by(move) |> slice_max(RSS_diff, n = 1) |> ungroup() |> slice_head(n = 3) |> pull(protein) ## Check that we have 3 accessions movers ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Q9CQE7" "Q99M28" "P27661" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Plot profiles of movers plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = movers, labels = c("basal", "insulin")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){width=1152} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Plot maps of movers par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal") highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = c("black", "brown", "yellow"), pch = 21:23, cex = 1.5) plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin") highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = c("black", "brown", "yellow"), pch = 21:23, cex = 1.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-36-2.png){width=1152} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Add legend par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)) plot.new() legend("center", legend = movers, pch = 21:23, pt.bg = c("black", "brown", "yellow"), col = "black", pt.cex = 1.6, ncol = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-36-3.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ::: ::: ### Visualising overall trends There are several different ways we can visualise the overall movement trend of these proteins. The `bandle` package has functions to generate alluvial (also known as Sankey) and chord (also known as circos) plots to capture the flow of proteins between conditions. Let's load the `bandle` package. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library("bandle") ``` ::: The `plotTranslocations` function takes a list of two `MSnSet`s, one per condition, and a feature data column giving the localisation of each protein in each condition. Our `basal` and `insulin` objects already contain the localisations in their `final.localisation` column, so we simply subset them to our candidates (here all proteins passing either test). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Extract candidates from both conditions msnset_cands <- list(basal[candidates$protein, ], insulin[candidates$protein, ]) ## Check the number of proteins in each object lapply(msnset_cands, nrow) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] 963 [[2]] [1] 963 ``` ::: ::: Next, we set a colour scheme for the subcellular classes, with `"unknown"` in grey, and pass `msnset_cands` to `plotTranslocations`, specifying the `fcol` containing the localisations. The default plot generated by `plotTranslocations` is an alluvial plot, which uses code from the `ggalluvial` R package. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Set the colours of the plot to match the organelles mrkCl <- getMarkerClasses(basal, fcol = "markers") cols <- c(getStockcol()[seq(mrkCl)], "grey") names(cols) <- c(mrkCl, "unknown") ## Plot the flow of proteins alluvial <- plotTranslocations(params = msnset_cands, fcol = "final.localisation", col = cols) alluvial + ggtitle("Differential localisation: basal to insulin") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: The same information can be shown as a chord diagram by setting `type = "chord"`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plotTranslocations(params = msnset_cands, fcol = "final.localisation", col = cols, type = "chord") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P3_01_sandle_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Proteins that stay in the same compartment, including those that are `"unknown"` in both conditions, appear as flows from a compartment to itself. To focus on proteins whose localisation changes, subset `candidates` with `filter(loc_basal != loc_insulin)` before building `msnset_cands`. ## Interpreting the results Computational prediction of differential localisation is largely **exploratory**. LOPIT data contains noise between fractions and replicates, and some proteins naturally sit between organelles or in several at once. The results should be used as a starting point for further investigation (for example, searching the literature for evidence of movement, imaging, or biochemical follow-up), rather than as validation in themselves. Some things to keep in mind: * **Localisation and movement are separate questions.** A classification tells us where a protein is in each condition; SANDLE tells us whether it moves. A protein can move without changing its localisation, and a change in localisation near a threshold is not, on its own, evidence of movement. * **Markers are assumed not to move.** If a marker protein does relocate, the marker-based test cannot detect it, and it may distort both the classification and the niche model. The marker-free test does not have this limitation, but it also flags consistent shifts of whole compartments between conditions, as we saw in Challenge 4. * **Many movers are `"unknown"`.** Proteins that move often do not sit neatly within one compartment. Movements to and from `"unknown"` are real results, not failures, but they need careful checking of the profiles. * **Results depend on data quality.** Poorly resolved compartments lead to uncertain assignments, which in turn inflate DL probabilities. Always check resolution first. * **The marker-based test has a random component.** The robust fitting step uses random subsampling, particularly for niches with few markers. Set a seed for reproducibility, and treat proteins close to a threshold with caution. * **Thresholds are your choice.** This applies to the localisations, the DL probability and the FDR. Requiring both a high DL probability and a low FDR gives a short list supported by two kinds of evidence. Using either test, or looser thresholds, gives a longer list for exploration. Choose based on your question and how you will follow up the candidates. ::: {.callout-tip} #### Key Points * A protein is **differentially localised** if it changes subcellular niche between conditions, seen as a change in the *shape* of its profile across fractions. * We answer two separate questions: **where** each protein is in each condition, from a classification such as the published localisations or an SVM, and **whether** it moves, using SANDLE. * **SANDLE** detects differential localisation in seconds, with no priors, MCMC or HPC, making it a fast and robust alternative to BANDLE. * The **marker-based** test models each niche with a robust *t*-distribution and gives a **DL probability**. The **marker-free** test compares profiles between conditions and gives a **p-value and FDR** without needing any markers. * Combining the SANDLE scores with the localisations shows where the movers go. Many move to or from `"unknown"`, reflecting proteins that sit between compartments or in more than one location. * How to threshold, and on which test, is up to you: stringent for a short list, looser for exploration. Candidates should always be checked by plotting profiles and spatial maps, and followed up experimentally. ::: ## References
